Urgent referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy

Not the treatment for choroidal neovascularisation.
Reassure and review in six months
Delay costs central vision that treatment could save.
The lens is not the problem.

Prescribe patching of the right eye
Delay risks irreversible amblyopia and, if it is a tumour, far worse.
Correct. An absent red reflex demands urgent assessment — cataract and retinoblastoma both present this way.
Does not address the ocular finding.

Bruising and swelling, without restricted upgaze or bradycardia.
Would not produce bradycardia or restricted upgaze.
Inferior rectus entrapment in a floor fracture
Correct. Restricted upgaze with severe pain and AUTONOMIC DISTURBANCE — bradycardia and vomiting on attempted movement — is the entrapment picture.
Photophobia and cells, without the autonomic disturbance.

Continue lid hygiene alone for three months

Not the named escalation for this condition.

Thirty minutes, and thyroid function must be checked

Immediately, and it requires general anaesthesia
It is an outpatient procedure without anaesthesia.

Elevates the lid rather than moving the globe.

Depresses the eye and is supplied by the third nerve.

Discharge with topical antibiotic eye drops
There is no infection, and discharge would be sight-threatening.
X-ray to rule out a foreign body
There is no history of trauma.
Dilating the pupil would worsen the angle closure — actively dangerous here.
The headache and vomiting are ocular in origin, not meningeal.

Correct. Watery discharge, follicles, a tender preauricular node, and one eye then the other after a cold.

Thick discharge, usually unilateral, and typically without a node.

Thyroid disease causes proptosis rather than scleritis.

Relevant to chlamydial conjunctivitis, not scleritis.

Refractive correction is available at any age.

A.q: A 78-year-old woman complains of a constant foreign body sensation in the right eye. Examination shows the lower lid margin turned inward, with the lashes resting against the globe, and conjunctival injection. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Misdirected lashes can occur without the lid itself rotating; here the lid margin is turned in.
Inflamed lid margins with crusting at the lash bases, without inward rotation.
Excess folds of lid skin, which produces heaviness rather than lashes against the cornea.
The lid margin turns OUT, exposing the inner surface and producing TEARING rather than a foreign body sensation.

A.q: A 31-year-old woman has had a painless, firm nodule in her upper lid for six weeks. Warm compresses and lid massage for a month have not reduced it. Vision is unaffected. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue warm compresses for a further six months
Improvement can take months, but a lesion persisting beyond two to three months warrants referral rather than more of the same.
Incise and drain it in clinic
Incision and drainage is the hordeolum pathway; a chalazion is curetted or injected by ophthalmology.
A chalazion is a STERILE gland obstruction, so antibiotics do not address it.
Refer to ophthalmology for steroid injection or curettage
Correct. Conservative measures come first; a lesion that has not resolved goes on for intralesional steroid or curettage.
Excise the whole lid lesion under general anaesthetic
Disproportionate to a lesion managed with injection or curettage.

Associated with cataract and raised pressure.

Irrigation does not dislodge an embedded fragment.
Does not address the retained fragment.
Leave it and review in a week
Retained metal and rust cause ongoing inflammation.
Remove it and the rust ring, then antibiotics
Correct — the rust ring is removed too, as it perpetuates inflammation.

A.q: An 18-year-old woman has had a swelling of her left upper eyelid for 10 days. For the first day or two it was red and mildly painful; it is now painless but has grown. There has been no drainage, no change in vision and no itching. She has been well otherwise. Vital signs are normal, extraocular movements are intact and the pupils are equal and reactive. The left upper lid carries a 1.5 cm round, non-tender, mildly erythematous mass with no drainage. The underside of the lid is greyish-red. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: An acute staphylococcal infection of a lid gland. It appears within about 24 hours and stays TENDER, where this became painless as it grew.
Inflammation of the lacrimal gland, which swells the LATERAL third of the UPPER lid with a preauricular node.
Correct. A sterile obstruction of a meibomian gland: it builds over days to weeks and the mature lesion is NON-tender, which is what the painless second week tells you.
Inflammation of the lid MARGIN with crusting at the lash bases and a frothy tear film, not a discrete 1.5 cm nodule.
Infection of the lacrimal sac, which swells the NASAL aspect of the LOWER lid below the medial canthal tendon and expresses pus from the punctum.
A.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 20

The pathology here is corneal, not retinal.

A later concern rather than the reason for close monitoring.
Not the expected complication of blood in the chamber.

A large fixed pupil, worse in light.
Bilateral small irregular pupils with light-near dissociation.
The affected pupil fails to constrict, so the difference grows in LIGHT.

Instil topical anaesthetic and examine under pressure
Any pressure on the globe is contraindicated.
Rigid shield, nil by mouth, urgent referral
Correct. Nothing that raises intraocular pressure, and no pressure on the eye. Antiemetics as well, to stop straining.

So the patient does not strain

To reduce the risk of infection
